name: Ivan Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to AI companies, employers or government. This stays confidential. What is an ordinary workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sing for a chamber choir, record demo vocals at a studio and teach voice at a music school. I’m 27, trained through a music master’s and often lead the warm-up because I know where the singers need a breath.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work do you value, and what tests your patience?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A singer who finally releases a tight jaw is worth the long rehearsal. Studio dates get moved with little warning, and I have learned to check the booking fee before I relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AI Plateau will mostly change the office messages, not our singing. The music school still has pupils booked for voice lessons, and the studio wants a singer in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have eight months of bills saved and earn a decent rate, so I am not worried about next month’s rent. I have never used an AI tool; I prefer the paper score where I can mark a breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the Tuesday school lessons and the four studio dates on my calendar. This week I’d ask the school office to confirm next term’s paid hours in writing, then leave the savings alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. The usual nuisance is a client rescheduling a take, not a collapse in singing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a rescheduled take cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Usually a rescheduled take costs nothing if the studio honors the booking fee. I still check the agreement before counting that payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the school’s new AI calendar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let the office use its own calendar, but I would keep my paper list. My pupil records stay with the school, not with an app on my phone.

I would let the office shorten **messages** while keeping bookings clear in writing.
think: Eight months of **savings** and a decent rate make rent secure for now.
I prefer a **paper score** and have never used an AI tool myself.
do: Keep Tuesday **voice lessons** and four booked studio dates.
Confirm next term’s paid **school hours** in writing before counting them as income.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and rent in this mild picture.
fieldNote: His **reserve** and firm fees make a rescheduled take tolerable if the booking agreement pays.
He resists AI tools and protects **pupil records** through the school’s existing process.

steps.text: Keep Tuesday voice lessons and four booked studio dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir Steady Disruption could take some demo singing and the paperwork around bookings. I would ask the studio what it still pays a person to sing, not guess from a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quick demo tracks are a real part of my income, and the studio could buy a generated voice instead. Eight months of savings help, but I would not call a lasting cut harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio manager this week for the next quarter’s paid demo schedule. If two demo days disappear in the first year, I’d apply for an open voice-coach slot at another school, but only if the posted rate is at least my current lesson rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the demo income. I do not want to spend my reserve pretending the studio calls will return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why two days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two lost demo days would remove enough pay to cover my practice room for a month. One cancellation may be a client problem; two would change the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to compete for demos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would rather sing for clients who want my voice and keep teaching. I would not put a pupil’s recording into a tool just to chase a cheaper fee.

say: I’d ask the studio which **demo singing** still gets a human fee.
I would tell the choir to check **booking paperwork** before assuming every call is secure.
think: Two lost **demo days** could remove a month of practice-room rent.
Eight months of **savings** help, but a lasting cut would still change my work.
do: Ask the **studio manager** this week for next quarter’s paid demo schedule.
Apply for an open **voice-coach slot** if two demo days disappear and the posted rate matches my lesson rate.
feel: I feel **anxious** about studio income despite my reserve.
fieldNote: His response is to test a **paid vacancy**, not adopt a tool he distrusts.
He gives a specific **two-day** threshold and a rate condition before changing schools.
S1.quote: I do not want to spend my reserve pretending the studio calls will return.

steps.text: Ask studio manager for next quarter paid demo schedule
Apply for open voice-coach slot if two demo days vanish and rate matches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AGI by 2028 could replace demo recording, scheduling and lesson plans quickly. Robots able to do hands-on work as well as people would come around 2031, so live singing faces a later threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio might stop booking my voice in 2028, and some families could try AI lessons. Eight months of savings would buy time, but losing both kinds of work could eat it faster than I expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the school now for its written paid-hour commitment and ask two nearby schools about posted voice vacancies. If studio calls stop in the first year after 2028, I’d cancel my outside practice room at its next renewal and apply for a vacancy only at a clear paid rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious if studio bookings stopped and I had to use the reserve while finding more lessons. I would be alarmed if school hours fell too, because both pay sources would be shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I live alone, so no partner is paying my flat rent. I would tell my mother I have the reserve and a list of schools to contact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave singing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait until I knew a paid teaching slot existed. My music master’s and years of work belong in a classroom if the studio shuts its door.

say: I’d warn that **demo work** faces thinking AGI in 2028 before capable robots around 2031.
I would ask the school for a written **hour commitment** rather than promise safety.
think: Studio calls and some **lesson demand** could fall together after 2028.
My **eight-month reserve** buys time, but not a lifetime without paid work.
do: Get the school’s written **paid hours** now and ask two nearby schools about posted openings.
Cancel the outside **practice room** at renewal if studio calls stop after 2028; apply only for a clearly paid vacancy.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing studio income; a double loss with school hours would alarm me.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 recorded work** from the later 2031 robot threat to physical singing.
His nearby **vacancy search** needs a posted opening and clear pay; he will not leave paid lessons first.
S2.quote: My music master’s and years of work belong in a classroom if the studio shuts its door.

steps.text: Confirm current school paid teaching hours now
Cancel outside practice room at renewal if studio calls stop after 2028
Apply for posted voice vacancy if studio stops and pay is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AGI by 2031 gives us five years to see what happens to demo jobs. Capable robots for hands-on performance would follow around 2034, so I would keep the live choir calendar separate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could shift toward teaching without rushing into another degree. There are several nearby schools, but a vacancy matters only if it pays enough and pupils actually enroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the current school next term whether it will fund an extra voice group, with a room and a written rate. If the school approves it and six pupils pay, I’d run one term; in the first year after 2031, I’d renew only if the same fees cover the room and my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the studio work but less frightened than in the fast picture. Five years lets me test a group and keep most savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why six pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six fees cover the room and one paid evening for me. A full classroom is no success if the teacher goes home unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the choir to recruit for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might tell choir families about the class after the school approves it. I would not pressure children already struggling to afford lessons.

say: I’d tell the choir **demo jobs** face 2031 AGI before capable playing robots around 2034.
I would keep the live **choir calendar** separate from studio work.
think: A shift toward **teaching** could work if a nearby school has real paid demand.
I will not spend the **reserve** on another degree before testing pupils and a room.
do: Ask the current **school** next term for a funded group, an open room and written rate.
Run one **voice group** only with approval and six paying pupils; renew after 2031 only while fees cover room and hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about demos, but five years gives me room to test teaching.
fieldNote: He prefers a familiar **school setting** over new technology or another costly degree.
The group depends on **school funding**, six paid pupils and a rate that covers his teaching hours.
S3.quote: A full classroom is no success if the teacher goes home unpaid.

steps.text: Keep current school lessons while seeking funded group room and rate
Run voice group with approval and six paid pupils; renew after 2031 if fees cover costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make sensible plans. Thinking work changes in 2036 and capable robots for hands-on singing arrive around 2039; no one can promise the audience beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I might have stronger school hours and still sing studio parts, but I cannot count on either forever. The eight-month reserve and nearby schools mean I can move carefully instead of chasing every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the current school and studio contracts this year, and save one fifth of each paid demo fee after taxes. In the first year after 2036, I’d review actual school enrollments before signing another practice-room lease, and apply elsewhere only if a paid opening exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about the far end of that decade, but my job and income look secure over the next few years. I can take one measured step each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire from performances by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 in 2036, not retired from singing. I would still perform while clients pay a fair fee and my voice holds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does fair mean here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee must cover my travel and rehearsal time, not only the hour at the microphone. I would ask for the number in writing.

say: I’d tell the choir a **decade** permits measured plans before thinking AGI in 2036.
I would not promise **audiences** after capable performance robots arrive around 2039.
think: My **eight-month reserve** and nearby schools make the next few years manageable.
I cannot count on **studio fees** or teaching enrollment forever.
do: Keep current **school and studio** contracts and save one fifth of paid demo fees after tax.
Review **enrollment** before renewing a practice-room lease after 2036; apply elsewhere only for a paid opening.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later work, though near-term income remains secure.
fieldNote: His strong **reserve** supports caution, while his resistance to AI tools remains intact.
A new **school application** requires a paid opening; he does not assume a vacancy exists.
S4.quote: I would be 37 in 2036, not retired from singing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because demos and perhaps school hours could fall together. Written paid hours, a real teaching vacancy nearby and a room for lessons would help me replace work if clients leave.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask why I still keep a pencil in every score. I can change a phrase in a rehearsal without asking a screen, and I want to keep that habit while it serves the singers.

headlineQuote: I can change a phrase in a rehearsal without asking a screen, and I want to keep that habit while it serves the singers.
portrait: At **27**, Ivan sings in a chamber choir, records demos and teaches voice after a music master’s degree.
His high **pay**, eight-month reserve and nearby schools make short gaps manageable.
He avoids **AI tools** and relies on paper scores, clear fees and familiar school settings.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens demos and possibly lessons first; he seeks real vacancies before moving work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut both studio demos and school lesson hours.
whatWouldHelp: Written **school hours**, a paid nearby vacancy and an approved teaching room would help him replace lost work.
